title: Wicker Park
full_review:
In "Wicker Park" (MGM), heartthrob Josh Hartnett plays a young advertising executive obsessed with finding out why the girl of his dreams took off without so much as a kiss goodbye, let alone an explanation or forwarding address.
Set in Chicago, the movie -- a remake of the French film "L'Appartement" -- awkwardly shifts gears between romantic melodrama and suspense, neither providing enough emotional torque to power the story in its uphill battle against the overall lackluster material.

Taking its title from the well-known Windy City common, "Wicker Park" centers on Matthew (Hartnett), nursing a broken heart after his dancer girlfriend, Lisa (Diane Kruger), left him.
Returning to Chicago after spending two years in New York, Matthew, yuppified and engaged to his boss' sister (Jessica Pare), has tried to move on with his life. But on the eve of flying to China to close an important business deal, Matthew catches a chance glimpse of a girl he thinks is Lisa in a crowded restaurant.

The serendipitous sighting forces Matthew to make a choice: skip Shanghai and jeopardize his future along with his relationship with his fiancee, or board the plane and risk losing his one chance to resolve the nagging questions which have been gnawing away at him since the day Lisa hightailed it out of his life.
Needless to say, he opts for the former. But what starts out as a search for answers becomes a vortex of deception and emotional duplicity as he begins to unravel the mystery of Lisa's vanishing act. Of course, all this sounds much more interesting than it really is.

The likable Matthew Lillard plays Luke, the stock "best friend" whose new girlfriend, Alex (Rose Byrne, the film's sole performance bright spot), harbors an obsession of her own and quite literally holds the key to finding Lisa.

Director Paul McGuigan shuttles the action between past and present, weaving in memories of events from different characters' perspectives, as he pieces together the jigsaw puzzle. Many of the story's tangled threads lead to dead ends, with characters falling out of the script midway through, never to be seen or heard of again.

Ironically, the movie which hinges on questions of identity -- mistaken, stolen, etc. -- suffers from its own identity crisis. "Wicker Park" starts off as a love story before becoming a psychological drama, borrowing story elements from "Single White Female." But just when you think that it might head down the "Fatal Attraction" route -- cross your fingers that Matthew doesn't have a pet rabbit -- it once again switches back into conventional romance mode, replete with an appointed rendezvous in the eponymous park a la "An Affair to Remember."

To his credit, McGuigan exercises restraint during the film's several bedroom scenes, though they are a bit racy for its PG-13 rating. The movie touches on themes of truth, trust, envy and self-image, but to characterize its treatment of these issues as anything but superficial would be a stretch.

Still, even though viewers are likely to see most of the script's "surprise" twists coming, the nonlinear plot does arouse enough mild curiosity to make a stroll through "Wicker Park" a mildly diverting if not wholly satisfying experience.

Due to several sexual encounters, as well as sporadic crude language and humor, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
